forces: Piano; the cycle was written for two-manual harpsichord
intro: Shelley Katz plays the Aria that opens the Goldberg Variations: a richly ornamented tune above a bass that takes its time. Those quiet bass notes will support thirty variations before the Aria returns.

sections.label: A · G major towards D major
sections.mNote: The bass descends beneath the decorated tune

sections.label: A′ · The first sixteen bars again
B · Through E minor to G
sections.mNote: The bass takes a new route to the home key

sections.label: B′ · The second half again
sections.mNote: The minor-key passage returns before the final G-major cadence

cues.title: The bass takes its time
cues.text: The right hand curls around its melody with trills and leaning notes. Below it, the bass descends G–F♯–E–D, one step per bar. Bach builds the thirty variations that follow on this bass and its harmonies; the ornate tune belongs to the Aria.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 1–4; Mutopia edition, https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=979. The cycle’s bass foundation is discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A sleepless count
cues.text: In the story Forkel tells in his 1802 biography, Count Keyserlingk cannot sleep. Goldberg waits in an adjoining room to play for him, and Bach supplies the variations. The count rewards Bach with a golden cup filled with a hundred louis d’or.
cues.evidence: Johann Nikolaus Forkel, Bach biography (1802), anecdote quoted at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations. The commission story is disputed; the 1741 title page has no dedication to Keyserlingk.

cues.title: G returns beneath the ornaments
cues.text: After a cadence in D major, the first half starts again on G. The slow descending bass returns beneath the decorated melody. These sixteen bars get a second telling before the Aria moves on.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 1–16 and first repeat; Mutopia edition, music ID 979. Both halves repeat in this recording.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A turn towards E minor
cues.text: The second half begins over D, then moves towards E minor. The melody keeps its ornaments, but the bass is more restless now. It takes eight bars to reach the E-minor cadence, then another eight to find G major again.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 17–32: E-minor cadence in bar 24 and G-major close in bar 32. Mutopia edition, music ID 979.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Anna Magdalena’s two pages
cues.text: Anna Magdalena copies the Aria into two blank pages of her music notebook. The book begins in 1725; the handwriting places this entry around 1740. The music sits among the pieces collected and played in the Bach household.
cues.evidence: Christoph Wolff’s dating of Anna Magdalena’s copy, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations, Publication section. The approximate date concerns the copy.

cues.title: The second half starts again
cues.text: The G-major cadence sends the pianist back to the second half. Its E-minor passage returns, followed by the longer runs towards home. The final G sits beneath a fermata, with the melody still turning gently around it.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, second repeat of bars 17–32; final fermata and melodic ornament in bar 32. Mutopia edition, music ID 979.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From D major back to G
transitions.from: A · G major towards D major
transitions.to: A′ · The first sixteen bars again
transitions.how: The first half closes on a D-major chord, with D in the bass. The repeat returns directly to the opening G. Above the renewed G–F♯–E–D bass descent, the right hand begins its ornamented melody again.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bar 16 and repeat to bars 1–4; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

transitions.title: The bass moves on from D
transitions.from: A′ · The first sixteen bars again
transitions.to: B · Through E minor to G
transitions.how: The D-major cadence ends the first half for the second time. The next bar keeps D in the bass, then moves down to C; the following bars turn towards E minor. The pianist keeps the same three-beat pulse and the right hand’s elaborate ornaments.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 16–24; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

transitions.title: G major, then the second half
transitions.from: B · Through E minor to G
transitions.how: The second half closes in G major, with a fermata over the final bar. Its repeat sends the pianist back to bar 17 and the bass D. The passage through E minor and the return to G major are heard a second time.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, Aria, bars 17–32 and second repeat; Mutopia edition, music ID 979.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education.

In 1703 Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and married his second cousin Maria Barbara. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
